name: Tashiding
tagline: The heart-shaped hill of the sacred Bumchu vase
meta_description: Tashiding guide: the 1641 hilltop monastery, Thongwa Rangdol chorten, the Bumchu festival, jeeps from Jorethang and Yuksom, homestays and costs.
summary: Tashiding is a small market village in West Sikkim, below a hilltop monastery founded in 1641 between the Rathong Chu and Rangeet rivers. Pilgrims come for the Thongwa Rangdol chorten and the Bumchu festival in February or March. It sits about 19 km from Yuksom, so most people see it on the way to or from there.

local_story.title: A monastery older than the kingdom
paras: Tashiding Monastery was founded in 1641, a year before the first Chogyal was crowned at Yuksom, by Ngadak Sempa Chempo, one of the three Tibetan lamas who would crown him. The name is usually translated as 'the devoted central glory'. The site is a steep, heart-shaped hill rising between two rivers, the Rathong Chu and the Rangeet. In 1717, during the reign of the third Chogyal, Chakdor Namgyal, the monastery was enlarged, and it grew into one of the most revered sites in Sikkim.

Its holiest object is not a building but a chorten. Thongwa Rangdol, among the many white chortens on the hilltop, is said to wash away the sins of anyone who simply looks at it, and its name is often read as 'saviour by mere sight'. Around the chortens lie long rows of mani stones, slabs carved with prayers such as Om Mani Padme Hum, added over generations by pilgrims and carvers. Walking among them clockwise, turning prayer wheels, is the heart of a visit.

Once a year, on the 14th and 15th days of the first Tibetan month, usually in February or March, Tashiding holds Bumchu. Monks open a sacred vase of water, kept sealed through the year, and read the level of the water as a forecast: full means plenty, low means scarcity, and murky is taken as a sign of trouble ahead. Pilgrims come from across Sikkim and from Nepal and Bhutan, and many carry a little of the blessed water home for family members who could not make the journey.

did_you_know: Tashiding Monastery was founded in 1641, a year before the first Chogyal's coronation at Yuksom, by Ngadak Sempa Chempo, one of the three lamas who crowned him.
The Thongwa Rangdol chorten at Tashiding is said to wash away the sins of anyone who simply looks at it; its name is read as 'saviour by mere sight'.

intro: Tashiding village is a short row of shops, eateries and houses on the road between Legship and Yuksom, at about 1,450 m. The monastery stands on the hill above, reached by a road and then a steep path with steps, prayer flags and chortens. From the top you look down on two river valleys and across to the ridges of Pelling and Ravangla. It is about 19 km and an hour from Yuksom, and roughly 40 km and 1.5–2 hours from Pelling.

Most visitors give Tashiding two or three hours on the way to or from Yuksom, and that is enough for the monastery and chortens. Stay a night if you come for Bumchu, or if you want an unhurried evening walk among the mani stones after the day visitors leave. Outside the festival the village is quiet and cheap, with simple lodges and homestays and good local food. Indians need no permit; foreign nationals need the Sikkim Restricted Area Permit.
facts: Jio and Airtel in the village; weaker on the hill
costs: Village homestay with dinner and breakfast

highlights.title: The hilltop monastery
highlights.text: Founded in 1641 and enlarged in 1717, Tashiding Monastery sits on a heart-shaped hill between the Rathong Chu and the Rangeet. The climb from the road takes 20–30 minutes on steps lined with prayer flags, and the view over both valleys is the reward.

highlights.title: Thongwa Rangdol chorten
highlights.text: Among the white chortens on the hilltop, Thongwa Rangdol is the one pilgrims seek out, believed to cleanse sins by sight alone. Walk around it clockwise as local people do, and spend a few minutes watching pilgrims of all ages make their rounds.

highlights.title: Fields of mani stones
highlights.text: Long rows of slabs carved with prayers line the hilltop, laid down over generations. Some are old and mossy, others freshly cut. Do not move or sit on them. Walking slowly past them, clockwise, is one of the quietest experiences in West Sikkim.

highlights.title: Bumchu festival
highlights.text: On the 14th–15th day of the first Tibetan month, usually February or March, monks open the sacred vase and read the year's fortune from its water. Thousands of pilgrims come from Sikkim, Nepal and Bhutan. Book rooms early and check dates before you travel.

highlights.title: Cardamom country around the village
highlights.text: The warm, damp slopes around Tashiding grow large cardamom under shade trees, and Sikkim is India's largest producer of it. From late summer into autumn you may see pods being harvested and smoke-dried in village kilns. Ask before walking into a farm.

how_to_reach.text: Jeeps for Yuksom from Jorethang pass through Legship and Tashiding, roughly ₹150–250 a seat to Tashiding and 2.5–3 hours. From Siliguri, take a jeep to Jorethang first (₹250–350). Most departures are before noon, so start early. Fares are indicative; check at the stand.

Tashiding is about 19 km and an hour south of Yuksom, and shared jeeps between Yuksom and Jorethang stop here. From Pelling it is about 40 km via Legship, 1.5–2 hours; a reserved car makes it an easy day trip along with Khecheopalri or Yuksom.

A small car from NJP or Bagdogra takes about 5.5–6.5 hours for roughly 145 km via Melli, Jorethang and Legship and costs about ₹5,500–7,000. The Teesta valley road has had long closures since the October 2023 flood, so check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: Tashiding has a few simple lodges and family homestays in and around the village, priced for pilgrims and trekkers at about ₹1,500–2,500 per person with dinner and breakfast. Rooms are basic but clean in most places, with hot water by bucket in cold months. During Bumchu every room fills with pilgrims, so book weeks ahead or stay in Yuksom or Pelling and come in early on the main day. At other times you can usually find a bed by asking in the village, but book ahead if you arrive late in the day.
tips: Climb to the monastery early in the morning or after 3 pm, when the stone steps are cooler and the hilltop is quieter.
Walk clockwise around chortens and mani stone walls, and never sit or step on the carved stones.
For Bumchu, check the exact dates on the Tibetan calendar, book rooms early and expect long queues for the blessing.
Carry cash from Jorethang, Gyalshing or Pelling; small-village ATMs are not reliable.
Combine Tashiding with Yuksom: shared jeeps between them are cheap, and the two together tell the whole founding story of Sikkim.

experiences.title: Climb to Tashiding Monastery on its hill
experiences.summary: Walk the prayer-flag steps up the heart-shaped hill to Tashiding Monastery, founded in 1641 between the Rathong Chu and the Rangeet. Visit the prayer halls, then sit on the edge of the hill and look down over two river valleys and across to Pelling.
body: The road from Tashiding village climbs towards the monastery, and the last stretch is on foot: a steep path with stone steps, prayer flags and small chortens, taking 20–30 minutes for most people. Go early, when the steps are in shade and the hill is quiet except for monks and a few villagers. Rest at the bends and look back; the views open up as you climb, with the Rathong Chu valley on one side and the Rangeet on the other.

The monastery was founded in 1641 by Ngadak Sempa Chempo, a year before he and two other lamas crowned the first Chogyal at Yuksom, and enlarged in 1717 under the third Chogyal, Chakdor Namgyal. It follows the Nyingma school, like most of Sikkim's old monasteries. The prayer halls may be open or locked depending on rituals and the time of day; if they are open, remove your shoes, move clockwise and ask before taking photographs of the murals or images.

After the halls, walk along the hilltop to the chortens and mani stones, then find a quiet spot on the edge of the hill. On a clear morning you can see the ridges of Pelling and Ravangla, and the two rivers far below on either side of the hill. Carry water and a snack, as there is little on top. Come down slowly; the steps are steep and worn, and hold a rail or stick if your knees complain.

faqs.q: How long is the climb to Tashiding Monastery?
faqs.a: From where vehicles stop, the steep path with steps takes about 20–30 minutes up for most people and a little less down. Allow two hours in all to see the halls, chortens and mani stones without rushing. Seniors can manage it slowly with rests, but should wear shoes with grip and carry water.

faqs.q: Is Tashiding Monastery open to tourists?
faqs.a: Yes. Visitors are welcome on the hilltop and around the chortens throughout the day. The prayer halls may be locked at times or reserved for rituals, so you may not always see inside. Dress modestly, remove shoes before entering halls, walk clockwise and ask before taking photographs of images or people.

faqs.q: Which school of Buddhism does Tashiding follow?
faqs.a: Tashiding belongs to the Nyingma school, the oldest of the four main schools of Tibetan Buddhism and the one most closely linked to Guru Rinpoche. Most of Sikkim's oldest monasteries, including Pemayangtse, Dubdi and Sanga Choeling, are also Nyingma, reflecting the lamas who founded the kingdom in the 1640s.

experiences.title: Thongwa Rangdol and the mani stone kora
experiences.summary: Join pilgrims on a slow clockwise circuit of the chortens and carved mani stones on Tashiding hill, pausing at Thongwa Rangdol, the chorten said to cleanse sins by sight alone. Late afternoon, after the day visitors have gone, is the best time.
body: A kora is a clockwise walk around a sacred place, and Tashiding's hilltop is made for it. Start near the main chortens, a group of white stupas of different sizes, some very old, some rebuilt. Among them is Thongwa Rangdol, the chorten pilgrims seek out because simply seeing it is said to cleanse sins. Its name is usually read as 'saviour by mere sight'. Ask a monk or pilgrim to point it out, as it is not always labelled.

Around the chortens run long walls and rows of mani stones, flat slabs carved with Om Mani Padme Hum and other prayers, many painted in white, red, yellow and blue. Some are covered in moss and lichen; others look recently cut. They have been added over generations by pilgrims who commission them for blessings or in memory of family members. Do not sit on them, step on them, or take any away; they are offerings, not souvenirs.

Walk at the pace of the pilgrims, who are often elderly villagers turning hand prayer wheels as they go. Keep the stones and chortens on your right. Many people make three circuits, or more on special days. Late afternoon is lovely, with long shadows across the stones and the valleys turning blue below. Leave before dark, as the steps down are steep, and drop a small note in a donation box if you would like to support the monastery.

faqs.q: What is a kora and how do we do it?
faqs.a: A kora is a clockwise walk around a sacred site, such as a chorten, monastery or mountain, performed as prayer. At Tashiding, walk slowly around the chortens and mani stones keeping them on your right, turning prayer wheels with your right hand. There is no fixed number of rounds; many people do three.

faqs.q: What are mani stones?
faqs.a: Mani stones are flat stones or slabs carved with Buddhist prayers, most often Om Mani Padme Hum, the mantra of compassion. They are placed at monasteries, passes and paths as offerings and blessings. At Tashiding they form long rows and walls built up over generations. Never move, sit on or take one.

faqs.q: Can we photograph the chortens at Tashiding?
faqs.a: Yes, the chortens and mani stones are outdoors and photography is generally fine. Be respectful: do not climb on chortens or stones for a better angle, keep to the clockwise direction even with a camera, and ask before photographing pilgrims at prayer. Late afternoon light is best for the stones.

experiences.title: Bumchu night with the pilgrims
experiences.best_time: 14th–15th day of the first Tibetan month (Feb–Mar)
experiences.summary: Once a year Tashiding's monks open a sealed vase of sacred water and read the coming year from its level. Join thousands of pilgrims from Sikkim, Nepal and Bhutan for the night of prayers, the reading and the blessing, and come prepared for crowds.
body: Bumchu means 'sacred vase', and the festival is held on the 14th and 15th days of the first month of the Tibetan calendar, which usually falls in February or March. Exact dates move each year with the lunar calendar, so check them well ahead. Pilgrims start arriving a day or two before, filling the village, the roads from Legship and Yuksom, and the hill itself, many of them families who have travelled from across Sikkim, Darjeeling, Nepal and Bhutan.

At the heart of the festival, monks open the vase, which has been sealed through the year, and examine the water. The folk reading is simple: a full vase means plenty, a low level means scarcity, and murky water warns of trouble. The result is announced to the crowd and quickly spreads through the hills. Some of the water is then shared out to pilgrims as a blessing, and the vase is sealed again until the next year.

Expect crowds, long waits, cold nights and very little personal space. Book a room weeks ahead, or stay in Yuksom or Pelling and come in early on the main day, as jeeps fill up and roads jam. Carry warm layers, food, water and a torch, and keep valuables close. Follow the directions of volunteers and monks, do not push for the blessing, and remember this is a religious occasion first; photography of rituals may be restricted.

faqs.q: When is the Bumchu festival at Tashiding?
faqs.a: Bumchu is held on the 14th and 15th days of the first month of the Tibetan lunar calendar, which usually falls in February or March. The Western dates change every year. Check the current year's dates with Sikkim Tourism, a local agent or your hotel before booking, and arrive a day early if you can.

faqs.q: Can tourists attend Bumchu?
faqs.a: Yes. Visitors of any faith are welcome to attend, as long as they behave respectfully. Dress modestly, follow the crowd's clockwise flow, keep your voice down during rituals and do not push for the blessing. Foreign nationals need the Sikkim Restricted Area Permit. Photography of some rituals may be restricted, so ask volunteers or monks.

faqs.q: Where should we stay for Bumchu?
faqs.a: Rooms in Tashiding fill weeks ahead with pilgrims, so book early, expect simple homestays and lodges, and expect prices a little above normal. Otherwise stay in Yuksom, about an hour away, or Pelling, 1.5–2 hours away, and reach Tashiding early in the morning before the roads jam with jeeps.

experiences.title: Cardamom farms and lanes below the monastery
experiences.summary: Walk the lanes and terraces around Tashiding, where large cardamom grows under shade trees on the damp slopes. In harvest season you may see the red pods picked and smoke-dried in village kilns. Ask before entering a farm, and end with tea and local food.
body: Sikkim is India's largest producer of large cardamom, the smoky spice also called black cardamom, and the slopes around Tashiding are part of that cardamom country. The plant grows in clumps under shade trees on damp hillsides, often near streams, and from a distance it looks like a forest floor of tall leaves. The pods grow at the base of the plant, close to the ground, and turn reddish brown when ripe. Harvest runs from late summer into autumn.

Walk out from the village along the lanes and field paths and ask locally which farms welcome visitors; a homestay host or a guide can introduce you. In harvest season you may see families cutting the pod clusters, carrying them in baskets, and drying them over wood fires in small kilns called bhattis, which gives the spice its smoky taste. Do not pick anything, keep to paths, and ask before photographing people at work. Leave a tip for anyone who spends time showing you around.

Cardamom has brought cash into West Sikkim for generations, but crops have suffered from plant disease and changing weather in recent decades, and many farmers now mix it with other crops. Ask about it over tea. Then eat in the village: a thali with rice, dal, local greens and a pickle, or momos and thukpa. Buy a small bag of cardamom from a village shop if you like, and check the price per kg first.

faqs.q: When is cardamom harvest season in Sikkim?
faqs.a: Large cardamom is harvested from roughly August to November, depending on altitude and the season's weather, with lower farms starting earlier. During these months you have the best chance of seeing pods picked and dried in village kilns. At other times you can still see the plants, but there is less activity.

faqs.q: Can we visit a cardamom farm near Tashiding?
faqs.a: There are no formal tours, but many farming families are happy to show visitors their plants if asked politely. Go through your homestay host or a local guide, who can introduce you and help with language. Keep to the paths, do not pick anything, and leave a small tip for your hosts' time.

faqs.q: Where can we buy cardamom in West Sikkim?
faqs.a: Village shops and markets in Tashiding, Yuksom, Gyalshing, Legship and Jorethang sell large cardamom, usually by weight. Prices change with the harvest and the market, so ask for the rate per kg and buy small amounts. Look for whole, dark, well-dried pods with a strong smoky smell.

faqs.q: How do we reach Tashiding?
faqs.a: From Siliguri, take a shared jeep to Jorethang (₹250–350), then a Yuksom-bound jeep via Legship, roughly ₹150–250 to Tashiding. From Yuksom it is about 19 km and an hour by shared jeep or car; from Pelling, about 40 km and 1.5–2 hours. A reserved car from NJP costs about ₹5,500–7,000. Fares are indicative.

faqs.q: What is the Bumchu festival?
faqs.a: Bumchu, meaning 'sacred vase', is Tashiding's yearly festival on the 14th and 15th days of the first Tibetan month, usually February or March. Monks open a sealed vase of holy water and read the coming year from its level, then share the water as a blessing. Thousands of pilgrims attend from Sikkim, Nepal and Bhutan.

faqs.q: How much time do we need at Tashiding?
faqs.a: Two to three hours is enough for the climb, the monastery, the chortens and mani stones on a normal day. Most people visit on the way to or from Yuksom. Stay a night if you want a slow evening kora after the day visitors leave, and one or two nights if you come for Bumchu.

faqs.q: Is Tashiding Monastery a difficult climb?
faqs.a: It is short but steep. After the road ends, a path with stone steps takes most people 20–30 minutes to the top. Go slowly, rest at the bends and carry water. Seniors can usually manage it with care. The steps can be slippery after rain, so wear shoes with grip.

faqs.q: What is special about Thongwa Rangdol?
faqs.a: Thongwa Rangdol is a chorten on Tashiding hill that pilgrims believe cleanses sins simply by being seen; its name is often read as 'saviour by mere sight'. It stands among other white chortens and long rows of carved mani stones. Walk around them clockwise, as local pilgrims do.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Tashiding?
faqs.a: February to May and October to November are best. Bumchu in February or March brings crowds and colour; spring and autumn bring clear, comfortable days for the climb. December and January are cold but quiet. June to September is wet, with leeches and landslide risks on the roads.

faqs.q: Where can we stay in Tashiding?
faqs.a: There are a few simple lodges and family homestays in and around the village, costing roughly ₹1,500–2,500 per person with dinner and breakfast. They are basic but friendly. During Bumchu they fill with pilgrims, so book early or stay in Yuksom or Pelling. At other times you can usually find a room by asking locally.

faqs.q: Do we need a permit to visit Tashiding?
faqs.a: Indian citizens need no permit for Tashiding. Foreign nationals need the Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, available online or at entry points such as Rangpo and Melli, which covers this part of West Sikkim. Carry passport and visa copies. Rules change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can we combine Tashiding with Yuksom and Pelling?
faqs.a: Yes, easily. A common loop is Pelling for two nights, Yuksom for one or two, and Tashiding on the way back down to Jorethang. Shared jeeps link Yuksom and Tashiding cheaply, and a reserved car can do Pelling, Khecheopalri, Yuksom and Tashiding over two relaxed days.
